Mining · Tanzania

Land change around mining licences in Tanzania

Gold, graphite and nickel projects in Tanzania sit next to villages and small-scale mining areas. We map what changes on the ground around them, such as new pits, cleared ground, tracks, structures and vegetation returning after rehabilitation. Each change is dated and measured against your licence boundary and buffers, reviewed by a person, and delivered to your land, environmental and community teams. We map land, not people.

Request a proposal See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

What changes at the edge of a licence

Large mining licences in Tanzania border villages, farmland and small-scale mining areas. Land at the edge of a licence changes between site visits, and each change raises a question for the land, environmental or community team.

“New pits have opened near the boundary.”

Pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps and water-filled excavations inside and around the licence area, mapped with their distance to the boundary and flagged when they are new between dated surveys.

“The land around the licence is filling up.”

New structures, cleared plots and tracks in a ring around the licence, and settlement growth near the fence line and access roads, compared year by year.

“What stands inside the tailings buffer?”

Structures inside the tailings, blast and buffer zones your engineers define, each listed with its distance to the source. We do not model dam breaks or blasts; the zone comes from your engineers.

“Is the rehabilitation working?”

How vegetation cover returns on rehabilitated pits, waste dumps and closed borrow areas, tracked between dates.

Who this is for

  • Mine land and tenure teams
  • Environmental and closure managers
  • Community-relations and grievance teams
  • Resettlement and valuation consultants
  • Lenders’ environmental and social monitors
  • Mining regulators, and technical-support partners of small-scale licence holders
  • ESIA consultancies and registered environmental experts

The law and the regulator

Licences, the Mining Commission and what occupation does not give

A summary of the public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice.

The Mining Act, Cap. 123, gives the Mining Commission (Tume ya Madini) the function to “regulate and monitor the mining industry” (s.22). It sets exclusive areas for primary licences (s.16) and the grant of primary mining licences (PMLs, leseni ndogo za uchimbaji madini) (s.55), and the local-content duties in Part VIII. Licence information is published on the Mining Cadastre Portal.

The courts have been clear that occupation does not create mineral rights. As summarised on TanzLII, the Court of Appeal held in 2018 that occupation or administrative promises do not ([2018] TZCA 225), and TanzLII’s summary of the 2024 appeal ([2024] TZCA 580) records that “a party cannot claim lawful ownership of mining property without a valid licence under the Mining Act, regardless of occupation or official correspondence”.

Small-scale licence areas

The Mining Commission oversees small-scale miners (wachimbaji wadogo), including licence holders who work under technical-support agreements under the Kanuni za Msaada wa Kiufundi kwa Wamiliki wa Leseni Ndogo za Uchimbaji Madini, 2025. It reported on 26 August 2026 that it had inspected 128 such projects, found 42 inactive and 86 with shortcomings, and given them 30 days to correct them; it may revoke technical-support approvals (Mining Commission, 26 August 2026).

Whether ground is being worked in a licence area, and what changed between two dates, is exactly what dated imagery shows. For regulators and technical-support partners, we map pits, disturbed ground, spoil and new tracks across small-scale licence areas and flag what is new between surveys, so inspections go where the ground has changed.

What we map around a licence

The boundary, the ring around it, and the zones inside

Boundary and perimeter change. We map new structures, cleared ground and new tracks inside the licence boundary and in a ring around it, and compare between dated surveys. New and removed features are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views. Fence lines and gates are too thin to detect on satellite imagery, so a reviewer checks them on drone imagery where it is flown.

Excavations. Pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps and water-filled excavations inside and around the licence area are mapped with their distance to the boundary, and new sites are flagged between dates. We describe the sites and the ground, never who is working them.

Hazard and buffer zones. Structures inside the tailings, blast or buffer zones your engineers define are listed with their location and distance to the source, so your team knows which structures stand inside a zone it is responsible for.

Rehabilitation. Vegetation cover on rehabilitated land is compared between dates from Copernicus Sentinel imagery and drone orthophotos, so the closure team can see the trend.

What you receive

  • A register of structures, excavations and tracks, with distances to the boundary or zone
  • New and removed features between surveys, with before-and-after views
  • Structures inside the zones your engineers define
  • Vegetation trends on rehabilitated land
  • Settlement growth around the licence
  • A PDF report in English, with GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

New projects and expansions

A dated baseline before the valuation

A new pit, plant or tailings facility often needs land that villages use. Tanzanian compensation follows the valuation: the Valuation and Valuers Registration Act treats payment as prompt only within six months after the valuation is approved (s.52), and the High Court has held that developments made after the valuation and notice are not compensable. On a lender-financed project, IFC Performance Standard 5 adds a publicly established cut-off date.

A dated structure register of the project area before the valuation, and another on the cut-off date, supports the census, the asset inventory and the valuation. It does not replace them, and it does not decide eligibility.

Imagery history

Where archived satellite imagery exists, the documented history of a licence area and its surroundings shows what was built, cleared or dug, and roughly when. How much archive exists varies by place and year. It is not a title, tenure or valuation check.

Resettlement cut-off-date baselines

A dated register of the structures in your project footprint at the cut-off date, to support your census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5.

Local content

How we work on Tanzanian mining contracts

The Mining (Local Content) Regulations, 2018 (GN 3 of 2018), as amended, set the rules for anyone supplying a mining licence holder or its contractors:

  • an indigenous Tanzanian company has at least 20 per cent of its equity owned by Tanzanian citizens, with Tanzanians in at least 80 per cent of executive and senior management posts and all other posts;
  • a non-indigenous company supplying “a contractor, a subcontractor, licensee, the Corporation or other allied entity” must “incorporate a joint venture company with an indigenous Tanzanian company and afford that indigenous Tanzanian company an equity participation of at least twenty percentum” (reg 8(6));
  • sole-sourced contracts, and competitive contracts above a set value, are notified to the Commission (reg 16);
  • since 2022, “contractor” and “mining activities” cover activities “within and outside Tanzania”.

Each mining proposal sets out how it meets reg 8(6): the indigenous Tanzanian company and its equity share. The regulations have been amended several times, so check the current text with the Mining Commission or your counsel before a contract is signed.

Where to check

  • The Mining Commission’s regulations page
  • The Local Content and CSR system, LCCSR-MIS
  • Our notes for working with AfriScan in Tanzania

Drone surveys at mines

Orthophotos, volumes and fence checks, with the licence holder’s authority

Where satellite imagery is not detailed enough, drone surveys capture orthophotos and elevation models of pits, dumps, stockpiles and rehabilitation areas, with stockpile and earthworks volumes calculated from them, subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires. Volumes from drone models are not a statutory survey; where a registered surveyor is required, the data supports their work.

Flying over a licence area

Fly only for the licence holder or with its written authority, with the launch and recovery consents of GN 268 of 2026, reg 86, and within the 50 m rule for people and structures not under the operator’s control unless TCAA approves otherwise. Blasting is regulated under the mining laws. Afridrone is working towards Tanzanian drone approvals, and every drone proposal names the company that will fly.

Drone law in Tanzania

How it works

From licence file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the licence boundary, the zones your engineers define and what the record is for. We agree the ring width, the imagery, the dates and the deliverables in a written proposal, which also sets out how it meets reg 8(6) of the Mining (Local Content) Regulations.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Excavations, structures, tracks and cleared ground are mapped across the licence area and its surroundings from dated satellite imagery or the imagery you hold.

  3. Check up close

    Drone surveys capture the areas that need detail, subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result, and the report goes to the contacts you name with the GIS layers.

What this is, and what it is not

Land and assets only. We map sites, ground and structures visible from above, reviewed by a person. We never identify, count or follow people; we do not see underground workings, shafts under cover or anything at night; and the register is not a cadastral survey or a licence check. See the global mining page.

Frequently asked questions

Can you tell us who is digging near our licence boundary?

No. We map sites and ground, never people. The register shows where pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps and water-filled excavations are, how far each is from the boundary, and when it first appears between dated surveys. What a site is, and what to do about it, is for your teams, the Mining Commission and the authorities to establish.

Can you see underground workings or shafts?

No. Imagery shows the surface. Underground workings, and shafts under cover or roofs, are not visible from above, so the register lists only what can be seen and says where the imagery limits what can be shown.

Where do the licence boundaries come from?

From you. Send the licence coordinates or polygons from your licence documents, or the boundaries you hold from the Mining Cadastre Portal, and the tailings, blast or buffer zones your engineers define. We measure against those; we do not verify title or licence status.

Does occupation of land inside a licence area give mineral rights?

The Court of Appeal has held that it does not. TanzLII’s summary of the 2024 appeal ([2024] TZCA 580) records that “a party cannot claim lawful ownership of mining property without a valid licence under the Mining Act, regardless of occupation or official correspondence”, following an earlier decision to the same effect, as summarised on TanzLII ([2018] TZCA 225). A dated map records what was on the ground and when; whether anyone has a right is for the law to decide.

How do the mining local-content rules affect this service?

A non-indigenous company that supplies a contractor, a subcontractor or a licensee must form a joint venture with an indigenous Tanzanian company and give it at least 20 per cent of the equity (Mining (Local Content) Regulations, reg 8(6)). Each mining proposal sets out how it meets reg 8(6), naming the indigenous Tanzanian company and its equity share. Check the current text of the regulations, which have been amended several times, with the Mining Commission or your counsel.

Can you show rehabilitation progress for closure?

We track how vegetation cover returns on rehabilitated land between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel imagery and drone orthophotos where they are flown. It shows the trend; it is not an ecological assessment, a closure certificate or the regulator’s sign-off.

Send us the licence area and the zones that matter

The licence boundary and any tailings, blast or buffer zones (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile or GeoPackage), the region, and what the record is for: boundary change, a resettlement baseline, rehabilitation or small-scale licence areas. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal that sets out how it meets the mining local-content rules.
